dx: Traumatic rupture of the aortic isthmus after a high-speed car crash, with hemorrhagic shock
case: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after she was the restrained driver in a head-on collision at highway speed. She has severe chest pain that radiates to her back. Temperature is 36.2 °C (97.2 °F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 78/50 mmHg. Physical examination shows pale, cool, moist skin and a capillary refill time of 4 seconds. Hemoglobin concentration is 10.8 g/dL (12 to 16). A chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum and a left pleural effusion. CT angiography shows a tear of the descending thoracic aorta just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, with a large mediastinal hematoma and a left hemothorax. The diagnosis is traumatic rupture of the aortic isthmus with hemorrhagic shock.

questions.stem: Which of the following anatomic features best explains why sudden deceleration tore the aorta at this site?
options: The aortic media at the isthmus lacks elastic laminae
The arch is held fixed by the pericardium while the descending aorta swings freely
A mobile arch joins a descending aorta tethered at the ligamentum arteriosum
The isthmus has no vasa vasorum and is weakened by chronic ischemia
approach: Note the mechanism: sudden deceleration, where the heart and arch keep moving forward.
Find where a movable segment meets a fixed one: the isthmus, at the ligamentum arteriosum.
Shear stress is greatest at that junction, so the wall tears there.
questions.why: In a head-on crash, the heart and aortic arch keep moving forward when the body stops. The descending thoracic aorta is held in place by the ligamentum arteriosum (the remnant of the ductus arteriosus), the intercostal arteries, and the pleura. The isthmus, just distal to the left subclavian artery, is the junction between these mobile and fixed parts, so shear forces concentrate there. Most patients who reach the hospital alive have a contained tear held by the adventitia and mediastinal tissue.
whyNot: The aortic media is made of many elastic laminae along its whole length, including the isthmus. Elastic fiber loss is a feature of cystic medial degeneration in Marfan syndrome, not normal anatomy.
This reverses the anatomy. The heart and arch are the mobile parts, and the descending aorta is the fixed part.
Correct.
The thoracic aorta has vasa vasorum in its outer media and adventitia. Loss of vasa vasorum from endarteritis is the setting of syphilitic aortitis, which weakens the ascending aorta.

questions.stem: A pulmonary artery catheter is placed before surgery. Which of the following sets of hemodynamic findings is most likely?
options: Low cardiac output, high systemic vascular resistance, low wedge pressure
Low cardiac output, high systemic vascular resistance, high wedge pressure
High cardiac output, low systemic vascular resistance, low wedge pressure
Low cardiac output, low systemic vascular resistance, low wedge pressure
approach: Classify the shock: blood loss from a ruptured aorta is hypovolemic shock.
Low blood volume lowers preload, so the wedge pressure and cardiac output fall.
The baroreceptor reflex raises sympathetic tone, so systemic vascular resistance rises, which explains her cool, pale skin.
questions.why: In hypovolemic shock the primary problem is too little blood returning to the heart. Filling pressures fall, so the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is low, and stroke volume and cardiac output fall. Reflex sympathetic activation constricts arterioles, raising systemic vascular resistance and giving cool, clammy skin.
whyNot: Correct.
A high wedge pressure with low output and high resistance is cardiogenic shock, as after a large myocardial infarction. Here the pump is normal and the tank is empty.
High output with low resistance is early septic (distributive) shock, with warm, flushed skin. Her skin is cool and pale.

Low resistance with low filling pressure fits neurogenic shock after a high spinal cord injury, where loss of sympathetic tone causes warm skin and often bradycardia. She has tachycardia and cool skin.

questions.stem: On a graph that combines her cardiac function curve and her venous return curve, which of the following best describes the effect of the blood loss before any reflex response occurs?
options: The venous return curve rotates downward with the same x-intercept; cardiac output falls
The cardiac function curve shifts downward; right atrial pressure rises at the new point
The venous return curve shifts right; cardiac output and right atrial pressure both rise
The venous return curve shifts left; cardiac output and right atrial pressure both fall
approach: Blood loss lowers the mean systemic filling pressure, which is the x-intercept of the venous return curve.
A lower filling pressure moves the venous return curve to the left without changing its slope.
The new intersection with the unchanged cardiac function curve lies at a lower cardiac output and a lower right atrial pressure.
questions.why: Mean systemic filling pressure depends on blood volume relative to vascular capacity. Hemorrhage lowers it, so the venous return curve shifts left in parallel. The cardiac function curve has not changed, so the two curves now cross at a lower right atrial pressure and a lower cardiac output. Reflex venoconstriction later shifts the venous return curve partly back to the right.
whyNot: A downward rotation with the same x-intercept is caused by a rise in total peripheral resistance, as with arteriolar constriction. Blood loss changes the intercept itself.
A downward shift of the cardiac function curve means reduced contractility, as in heart failure. Her heart muscle is not the primary problem.
A rightward shift happens with volume infusion or venoconstriction. It is the response to treatment, not the effect of hemorrhage.
Correct.

topics: Cardiac function and venous return curves

questions.stem: In the intensive care unit, her O2 consumption is 240 mL/min, arterial O2 content is 14 mL O2/dL, and mixed venous O2 content is 6 mL O2/dL. Her heart rate is 125/min. Which of the following is closest to her stroke volume?
options: 14 mL
24 mL
40 mL
60 mL
approach: Use the Fick principle: cardiac output equals O2 consumption divided by the arteriovenous O2 difference.
The difference is 8 mL O2/dL, or 80 mL O2/L, so cardiac output is 240 divided by 80, or 3.0 L/min.
Stroke volume is cardiac output divided by heart rate: 3,000 mL/min divided by 125/min is 24 mL.
questions.why: The Fick principle states that the O2 taken up by the body each minute equals blood flow times the O2 removed from each liter of blood. Her low cardiac output means each liter of blood must give up more O2, so mixed venous content falls and the arteriovenous difference widens. A stroke volume of about 24 mL, far below the normal 60 to 100 mL, shows how much preload she has lost.
whyNot: This comes from dividing O2 consumption by the arterial O2 content alone (140 mL/L) instead of the arteriovenous difference.
Correct.
This is 3.0 L/min divided by a normal heart rate of 75/min. Her heart rate is 125/min.
This is a typical resting stroke volume in a healthy adult. It is not consistent with a cardiac output of 3.0 L/min at 125/min.

dx: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome with pre-excited atrial fibrillation
case: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of palpitations and lightheadedness that began suddenly 1 hour ago during soccer practice. Since age 14 he has had brief episodes of rapid, regular palpitations that stopped on their own. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is about 220/min and irregular, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mmHg. An ECG shows an irregularly irregular wide-complex tachycardia with QRS complexes that vary in width and shape and ventricular rates up to 280/min. After electrical cardioversion, an ECG shows sinus rhythm with a PR interval of 0.09 seconds (0.12 to 0.20), a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex, and a QRS duration of 0.13 seconds (under 0.12). The diagnosis is Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome with pre-excited atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the short PR interval and the slurred upstroke of the QRS complex on his ECG in sinus rhythm?
options: Rapid conduction through the AV node, then early activation of both bundle branches
An ectopic atrial focus near the AV node that fires just before the sinus node does
Delayed conduction in the left bundle, so the left ventricle is activated from the right
Bypass of AV nodal delay, then slow cell-to-cell spread from the pathway's insertion
approach: The PR interval is mostly the delay in the AV node, so a short PR means the impulse skipped that delay.
An accessory pathway connects atrium to ventricle directly and activates ventricular muscle early.
That early activation spreads slowly through working myocytes instead of the fast Purkinje system, which slurs the start of the QRS (the delta wave).
questions.why: In Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) crosses the atrioventricular groove. Atrial impulses reach the ventricle through it without the normal AV nodal delay, so the PR interval is short. The region near the pathway's insertion depolarizes first by slow muscle-to-muscle conduction, which produces the delta wave. The rest of the ventricle is then activated through the normal His-Purkinje route, and the QRS is a fusion of both fronts, so it is wide.
whyNot: Fast AV nodal conduction shortens the PR, but the ventricles are then activated normally through the His-Purkinje system, so the QRS stays narrow with no delta wave.
An ectopic atrial rhythm changes the P-wave shape and may shorten the PR slightly, but ventricular activation is normal and there is no delta wave.
Left bundle branch block widens the QRS, but the PR interval is normal and the upstroke is not preceded by early pre-excitation.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his arrhythmia carried a high risk of progressing to ventricular fibrillation?
options: Reentry within the ventricles around scar from a prior infarct
Atrial impulses crossing a pathway that lacks decremental conduction
Prolonged ventricular repolarization that allows early afterdepolarizations
Rapid firing of a single ectopic focus in the right ventricular outflow tract
approach: In atrial fibrillation the atria fire at 350 to 600 impulses per minute.
Normally the AV node conducts more slowly as impulses come faster (decremental conduction), which caps the ventricular rate.
An accessory pathway lacks this property, so it can pass impulses at very fast rates that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.
questions.why: The AV node protects the ventricles in atrial fibrillation because its conduction slows as impulse frequency rises. Most accessory pathways are made of ordinary myocardium with a short refractory period and no decremental slowing. In pre-excited atrial fibrillation, many impulses pass down the pathway, giving an irregular, wide-complex tachycardia with ventricular rates that can exceed 250/min. Rates that high can trigger ventricular fibrillation and sudden death.
whyNot: Scar-related reentry causes monomorphic ventricular tachycardia after myocardial infarction. He is 19 with no infarct, and his rhythm is irregular.
Correct.
Long repolarization with early afterdepolarizations triggers torsades de pointes in long QT syndrome. His problem is conduction, not repolarization.
Outflow tract ventricular tachycardia is regular and usually benign. It does not explain an irregular rhythm with varying QRS shapes.

topics: Decremental conduction in the AV node

questions.stem: An electrophysiology study finds his accessory pathway crossing the left atrioventricular groove at the lateral mitral annulus. In a normal heart, which of the following prevents atrial impulses from crossing to the ventricles at this site?
options: Fibrous rings of the cardiac skeleton around the valve openings
Epicardial fat in the atrioventricular groove that blocks conduction
Loss of gap junctions between all atrial and ventricular myocytes
The endocardium that covers the valve leaflets and chordae tendineae
approach: Atrial and ventricular muscle are separated at the atrioventricular junction.
The separating layer is dense connective tissue, the fibrous skeleton, which does not conduct impulses.
The only normal crossing point is the AV bundle, which pierces the central fibrous body; an accessory pathway is a muscle strand that crosses the rings elsewhere.
questions.why: The fibrous skeleton of the heart is made of four fibrous rings around the valves joined by the fibrous trigones. Dense collagen does not conduct electrical impulses, so it insulates the atria from the ventricles. Normally the impulse can pass only through the AV node and the AV bundle, which pierces the central fibrous body. In Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome a strand of muscle bridges the ring, and ablation at that site cures the condition.
whyNot: Correct.
Epicardial fat fills the atrioventricular groove around the coronary vessels, but it is not the electrical barrier. The fibrous rings are.
Gap junctions link cells within the atrial muscle and within the ventricular muscle. Atrial and ventricular myocytes do not touch across the rings, because the fibrous skeleton separates them.
The endocardium lines the chambers and covers the valves. It is a thin endothelial layer and does not insulate atria from ventricles.

questions.stem: During the procedure, contrast injected into the coronary sinus outlines its tributaries but does not outline the veins that drain the anterior wall of the right ventricle. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: These veins join the middle cardiac vein beyond the reach of the contrast
These veins empty into the left atrium as part of the smallest cardiac veins
These veins cross the right coronary groove and open into the right atrium
These veins drain into the great cardiac vein against the flow of contrast
approach: Most cardiac venous blood reaches the right atrium through the coronary sinus.
The great, middle, and small cardiac veins are its main tributaries, so they fill with contrast.
The anterior cardiac veins bypass the sinus and open directly into the right atrium, so they do not fill.
questions.why: The coronary sinus lies in the posterior atrioventricular groove and receives the great cardiac vein (with the anterior interventricular artery), the middle cardiac vein (with the posterior interventricular artery), and the small cardiac vein (with the right marginal artery). The anterior cardiac veins drain the anterior right ventricular wall, cross the right coronary groove, and open directly into the right atrium. The smallest cardiac veins open straight into the chambers, mostly on the right side. The coronary sinus also runs along the mitral annulus, which is why catheters placed in it can map left-sided accessory pathways.
whyNot: The middle cardiac vein runs in the posterior interventricular groove and drains the posterior walls of both ventricles. It is a coronary sinus tributary and would fill.
The smallest cardiac veins are tiny channels that open into the chamber they drain, mostly the right atrium and right ventricle. They are not the anterior right ventricular veins.
Correct.
The great cardiac vein drains the anterior left ventricle and septum along the anterior interventricular artery. Contrast in the coronary sinus fills it readily.

dx: Congenital long QT syndrome type 1 (KCNQ1) with torsades de pointes while swimming
case: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after she lost consciousness while swimming laps at a competition. A lifeguard pulled her from the pool, and she regained consciousness within 1 minute. She has fainted twice before during exercise. Her paternal uncle died suddenly at age 22 while swimming. Temperature is 36.6 °C (97.9 °F), pulse is 68/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mmHg. Serum potassium is 4.2 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), magnesium 2.0 mg/dL (1.7 to 2.2), and calcium 9.4 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5). A rhythm strip from the event shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QRS complexes twisting around the baseline. Her resting corrected QT interval is 520 ms (under 460). Genetic testing shows a heterozygous loss-of-function variant in KCNQ1. The diagnosis is congenital long QT syndrome type 1 with torsades de pointes.

questions.stem: Her younger brother was born with profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. His corrected QT interval is 590 ms, and he carries two loss-of-function KCNQ1 variants, one from each parent. Which of the following best describes the inheritance of his syndrome and the cause of his hearing loss?
options: Autosomal dominant; excess potassium entry that injures cochlear hair cells
Autosomal recessive; too little potassium secreted into the endolymph
X-linked recessive; loss of a sodium channel in the cochlear nerve
Autosomal recessive; abnormal collagen in the cochlear basilar membrane
approach: One altered KCNQ1 copy gives long QT without deafness (Romano-Ward, autosomal dominant), as in his sister.
Two altered copies give a longer QT plus deafness (Jervell and Lange-Nielsen), which is autosomal recessive.
The same KCNQ1 channel in the stria vascularis secretes potassium into the endolymph, which hair cells need to function.
questions.why: KCNQ1 encodes the pore-forming subunit of the slow delayed rectifier potassium channel (IKs). In the heart, loss of IKs delays repolarization. In the inner ear, the same channel in the stria vascularis pumps potassium into the endolymph, creating the high potassium concentration that drives hair cell transduction. One working copy is enough for hearing, so heterozygotes have long QT only, while people with no working copy have Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome with deafness and a more severe arrhythmia risk.
whyNot: His sister's Romano-Ward form is autosomal dominant, but deafness requires loss of both copies. The defect is too little potassium in the endolymph, not too much entry.
Correct.
KCNQ1 is on chromosome 11, not the X chromosome, and it encodes a potassium channel, not a sodium channel.
The inheritance is right, but collagen defects cause deafness in conditions such as Alport syndrome. KCNQ1 encodes an ion channel.

questions.stem: Her torsades de pointes is triggered by early afterdepolarizations that interrupt repolarization of the ventricular action potential. Which of the following ionic events most directly produces these afterdepolarizations?
options: Opening of fast sodium channels from a resting potential near -90 mV
A larger transient outward potassium current early in repolarization
A larger inward rectifier potassium current during electrical diastole
Reactivation of L-type calcium channels during a prolonged plateau
approach: Loss of the outward IKs current slows repolarization, so the plateau (phase 2) and phase 3 last longer.
During a long plateau, some L-type calcium channels recover from inactivation and open again.
The inward calcium current pushes the membrane potential back up before repolarization is complete, which is an early afterdepolarization.
questions.why: The plateau of the ventricular action potential is a balance between inward calcium current through L-type channels and outward potassium currents. When outward current is reduced, as in long QT syndrome type 1, the plateau lengthens. L-type channels then have time to recover and reopen, producing an inward current that depolarizes the cell again. If this reaches threshold in a group of cells, it triggers extra beats, and dispersion of repolarization across the wall lets them develop into torsades de pointes. Adrenergic surges, such as during swimming, make this more likely in type 1.
whyNot: Fast sodium channel opening causes the normal phase 0 upstroke from rest. An early afterdepolarization occurs during repolarization, when most sodium channels are inactivated.
More transient outward current would shorten the early part of repolarization. It would not cause a new depolarization during the plateau.
The inward rectifier holds the resting potential near -90 mV. More of it would stabilize the cell, not depolarize it.
Correct.

questions.stem: Early afterdepolarizations in long QT syndrome often arise in the specialized conducting cells beneath the endocardium. In a histologic section of the ventricular wall, which of the following features best identifies these cells?
options: Small cells with dense granules near the nucleus and sparse myofibrils
Narrow branched cells packed with myofibrils and linked by intercalated discs
Large pale cells rich in glycogen with few myofibrils at the periphery
Spindle cells with tapered central nuclei and no cross-striations
approach: The specialized conducting cells beneath the ventricular endocardium are Purkinje fibers.
Recall their histology: they are larger than working myocytes, with pale cytoplasm full of glycogen and only a few myofibrils near the cell edge.
Their large diameter supports fast conduction.
questions.why: Purkinje fibers lie in the subendocardial layer of the ventricles. They are wider than working myocytes, and their cytoplasm looks pale because it holds much glycogen and few myofibrils, which are pushed to the periphery. Their large diameter and many gap junctions give the fastest conduction in the heart. Purkinje fibers also have long action potentials, which is one reason early afterdepolarizations often start there.
whyNot: Cells with dense granules near the nucleus are atrial myocytes storing atrial natriuretic peptide. Atrial myocytes also have abundant myofibrils, and they are not in the ventricular subendocardium.
This describes working ventricular myocytes, which do the contractile work. They are narrower and packed with myofibrils.
Correct.
Spindle cells with central tapered nuclei and no striations are smooth muscle cells, such as those in the walls of coronary arteries.

questions.stem: Her resting ECG is recorded at the standard paper speed of 25 mm/s. Consecutive R waves are 22 small boxes apart. Which of the following best describes how her QT interval is measured and her heart rate on this tracing?
options: From QRS onset to T-wave end; about 68/min
From QRS end to T-wave end; about 68/min
From QRS onset to T-wave end; about 88/min
From P-wave onset to T-wave end; about 88/min
approach: At 25 mm/s each small box is 0.04 seconds, so 22 small boxes is 0.88 seconds.
Heart rate is 60 divided by the R-R interval in seconds: 60 divided by 0.88 is about 68/min (or 1,500 divided by 22 small boxes).
The QT interval runs from the start of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave, covering ventricular depolarization and repolarization.
questions.why: The QT interval measures the whole ventricular action potential, from the start of depolarization (QRS onset) to the end of repolarization (T-wave end). Because QT shortens as heart rate rises, it is corrected for rate, and her corrected value of 520 ms is clearly long. Her rate of about 68/min matches her measured pulse.
whyNot: Correct.
QRS end to T-wave end leaves out depolarization. The interval from the end of the QRS to the start of the T wave is the ST segment.
The measurement method is right, but 88/min comes from misreading 0.88 seconds as a rate. The R-R interval of 0.88 seconds gives about 68/min.
The P wave is atrial depolarization and is not part of the QT. The rate is also misread.

dx: Primary hyperaldosteronism from an adrenal adenoma, with hypokalemia and secondary hypertension
case: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician for follow-up of hypertension diagnosed 2 years ago that remains uncontrolled despite three medications, including a thiazide diuretic. She reports muscle weakness and leg cramps. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 168/102 mmHg. Physical examination shows no edema. Serum studies show sodium 144 mEq/L (135 to 145), potassium 2.8 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), and bicarbonate 32 mEq/L (22 to 28). Plasma aldosterone concentration is 32 ng/dL (4 to 21), and plasma renin activity is 0.2 ng/mL/h (0.6 to 4.3). CT shows a 1.6-cm left adrenal nodule, and adrenal vein sampling shows excess aldosterone from the left gland. The diagnosis is primary hyperaldosteronism from an adrenal adenoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes on her ECG is most likely to result from her current serum potassium concentration?
options: Flattened T waves with prominent U waves
Peaked T waves with a widened QRS complex
A shortened QT interval from a brief ST segment
A prolonged ST segment with an upright T wave
approach: Her potassium of 2.8 mEq/L is low.
Low extracellular potassium slows ventricular repolarization.
Slow repolarization flattens the T wave and makes a U wave visible after it.
questions.why: Hypokalemia reduces the outward potassium currents that repolarize the ventricle, so repolarization is slower and more spread out. On the ECG this flattens the T wave, may depress the ST segment, and shows a U wave. The T and U waves can merge, which looks like a long QT, and the risk of ventricular arrhythmias rises, especially in patients taking drugs such as digoxin.
whyNot: Correct.
Peaked T waves and a wide QRS are signs of hyperkalemia, as in renal failure. Her potassium is low.
A short QT from a short ST segment is the sign of hypercalcemia.
A long ST segment with a normal T wave is the pattern of hypocalcemia, as after loss of the parathyroid glands.

questions.stem: Despite her persistently high aldosterone concentration, she has no peripheral edema, and her serum sodium remains within the reference range. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Low renin that returns aldosterone secretion to normal levels
Increased ADH secretion that dilutes the extracellular fluid
Volume expansion raising ANP and pressure natriuresis
Loss of mineralocorticoid receptors from collecting duct cells
approach: Aldosterone makes the collecting duct reabsorb sodium, which expands extracellular volume at first.
The added volume stretches the atria and raises renal perfusion pressure.
Atrial natriuretic peptide and pressure natriuresis then increase sodium excretion, so volume stabilizes below the edema level (aldosterone escape).
questions.why: Aldosterone acts on principal cells to increase sodium channels (ENaC) and the Na+/K+ ATPase. Early on, sodium and water are retained. Within days, atrial stretch raises ANP, and higher renal perfusion pressure reduces proximal sodium reabsorption, so sodium excretion rises back to match intake. This escape limits volume expansion, which is why primary aldosteronism causes hypertension without edema. Potassium and hydrogen ion secretion do not escape, so hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis persist.
whyNot: Renin is suppressed, but her aldosterone is made by an autonomous adenoma that does not depend on renin, so it stays high.
More ADH would retain water and tend to cause hyponatremia and more volume. It does not explain the absence of edema.
Correct.
Receptor loss would stop all aldosterone effects, including potassium wasting. Her hypokalemia shows the receptors are still active.

questions.stem: Six months after removal of the left adrenal adenoma, her serum potassium and aldosterone-to-renin ratio are within the reference ranges, and she takes no medications. Her body mass index is 33 kg/m2, she drinks three glasses of wine each night, and her father has hypertension. Her blood pressure, averaged over two visits, is 134/86 mmHg. Using the 2017 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association categories, which of the following best describes her blood pressure now?
options: Elevated blood pressure from persistent aldosterone excess
Stage 1 hypertension from coexisting primary hypertension
Stage 2 hypertension from coexisting primary hypertension
Stage 1 hypertension from persistent aldosterone excess
approach: Classify the reading: systolic 130 to 139 or diastolic 80 to 89 mmHg is stage 1; 140/90 mmHg or higher is stage 2.
Her normal potassium and aldosterone-to-renin ratio show that the aldosterone excess has resolved.
Obesity, alcohol, and a family history are risk factors for polygenic primary hypertension, which often persists after the adenoma is removed.
questions.why: A reading of 134/86 mmHg is stage 1 hypertension. Her biochemical tests show the adenoma is cured, so the remaining hypertension is not from aldosterone. Primary (essential) hypertension is polygenic and is promoted by age, obesity, high sodium intake, and alcohol, all of which she has. Long-standing hypertension also remodels arterioles, which helps explain why many patients still need treatment after adrenalectomy.
whyNot: Elevated blood pressure is systolic 120 to 129 mmHg with diastolic under 80 mmHg. Her diastolic pressure is 86 mmHg, and her aldosterone excess has resolved.
Correct.
Stage 2 needs 140 mmHg systolic or 90 mmHg diastolic or higher. Her readings are below both.
The stage is right, but her normal potassium and aldosterone-to-renin ratio show the aldosterone excess is gone.

questions.stem: Before imaging was done, which of the following findings most strongly favored her diagnosis over renovascular hypertension from renal artery stenosis?
options: Hypokalemia with a metabolic alkalosis
An elevated plasma aldosterone level
Hypertension resistant to three drugs
Suppressed plasma renin activity
approach: Both conditions raise aldosterone, so both can cause hypokalemia, alkalosis, and resistant hypertension.
The difference is the source: in renal artery stenosis the kidney releases renin, so renin is high.
In primary aldosteronism the adrenal makes aldosterone on its own, and the high pressure and volume suppress renin.
questions.why: Renal artery stenosis lowers pressure at the juxtaglomerular cells, which release renin. Angiotensin II then drives aldosterone, so it is a high-renin, high-aldosterone state (secondary hyperaldosteronism). In primary aldosteronism the adenoma secretes aldosterone autonomously, sodium retention raises pressure, and renin is suppressed. A high aldosterone-to-renin ratio is therefore the screening test for primary aldosteronism.
whyNot: Hypokalemia and alkalosis come from any aldosterone excess, so they also occur with renal artery stenosis.
Aldosterone is high in both primary aldosteronism and renovascular hypertension, so this does not separate them.
Resistant hypertension is a reason to look for any secondary cause, including renal artery stenosis. It does not point to one.
Correct.

dx: Hypertensive emergency with papilledema and malignant nephrosclerosis
case: A 38-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of severe headache, blurred vision, and nausea for 1 day. He has a history of hypertension and stopped taking his medications 3 months ago. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 238/142 mmHg. Funduscopic examination shows bilateral optic disc swelling, flame-shaped hemorrhages, and cotton-wool spots. Serum creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3), up from 1.1 mg/dL a year ago. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein and red blood cells. A peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes. Echocardiography shows concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with a wall thickness of 15 mm (6 to 11). The diagnosis is hypertensive emergency with papilledema and malignant nephrosclerosis.

questions.stem: A renal biopsy is performed. Which of the following findings in his interlobular arteries and arterioles is most likely?
options: Homogeneous pink hyaline thickening with a narrowed lumen
Calcified rings in the media with an open lumen
Concentric smooth muscle layers with fibrinoid necrosis
Granulomas with giant cells disrupting the elastic lamina
approach: Severe, rapid rise in pressure with acute kidney injury and schistocytes means malignant (accelerated) hypertension.
Very high pressure injures the arteriolar wall acutely, causing fibrinoid necrosis.
Smooth muscle cells proliferate in layers with reduplicated basement membrane, giving an onion-skin pattern (hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis).
questions.why: In hypertensive emergency, arteriolar walls are damaged faster than they can adapt. Plasma proteins and fibrin seep into the wall (fibrinoid necrosis), and smooth muscle cells proliferate in concentric layers that narrow the lumen like an onion skin. The narrowed vessels cause renal ischemia, which raises renin and pressure further. Damaged endothelium also shears red cells, which explains the schistocytes.
whyNot: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is the lesion of chronic, milder hypertension and diabetes. It develops over years, not in a hypertensive emergency.
Medial calcification with an open lumen is Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis in older adults. It does not cause kidney injury.
Correct.
Granulomas with giant cells that break up the elastic lamina are seen in giant cell arteritis, which affects large arteries in older adults.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the cotton-wool spots seen on his funduscopic examination?
options: Swollen nerve fiber layer axons after arteriolar occlusion
Lipid and protein exudates leaking from damaged capillaries
Blood in the nerve fiber layer from ruptured arterioles
Swelling of the optic disc from raised intracranial pressure
approach: Cotton-wool spots are fluffy white patches in the superficial retina.
They form when a small arteriole closes and the retinal nerve fiber layer becomes ischemic.
Ischemia stops axoplasmic transport, and the axons swell with backed-up material, which is a small infarct.
questions.why: Hypertensive retinopathy reflects damage to the retinal arterioles. When very high pressure causes arteriolar occlusion, the nerve fiber layer it supplies becomes ischemic. Axoplasmic flow stops, and the swollen axon ends look like soft white spots with fuzzy edges. Along with flame hemorrhages and disc swelling, they mark severe, acute hypertensive damage.
whyNot: Correct.
Lipid and protein leakage forms hard exudates, which are sharp-edged yellow deposits. They are common in diabetic and chronic hypertensive retinopathy.
Bleeding in the nerve fiber layer forms flame-shaped hemorrhages, which he also has. They are red, not white.
Optic disc swelling is papilledema, which is a separate finding in this patient. It does not form scattered white spots in the retina.

questions.stem: Consider an abrupt rise in his aortic pressure while left ventricular preload and contractility stay constant. Compared with the beat before the rise, which of the following changes is most likely?
options: Stroke volume rises and end-systolic volume falls
Stroke volume rises and end-systolic volume rises
Stroke volume is unchanged and end-systolic volume falls
Stroke volume falls and end-systolic volume rises
approach: Higher aortic pressure means higher afterload: the ventricle must reach a higher pressure before the aortic valve opens.
With contractility unchanged, the end-systolic pressure-volume line is fixed, so ejection stops at a larger volume.
End-diastolic volume is unchanged, so a larger end-systolic volume means a smaller stroke volume.
questions.why: Stroke volume is end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume. When afterload rises, more of each contraction is spent raising pressure, and the fibers cannot shorten as far. Ejection ends at a higher pressure and a larger volume on the same end-systolic pressure-volume line, so stroke volume falls. Over the next few beats, the extra blood left behind raises preload and partly restores stroke volume through the Frank-Starling mechanism.
whyNot: This pattern follows a fall in afterload, as with arteriolar dilators. The ventricle empties more easily against a lower pressure.
End-systolic volume rises, but stroke volume cannot rise unless preload or contractility also rises.
An unchanged stroke volume with a smaller end-systolic volume would need a smaller end-diastolic volume, which is not part of this change.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the response of his ventricular myocytes to the long-standing pressure load that produced his left ventricular hypertrophy?
options: Re-entry into the cell cycle, adding new myocytes by mitosis
Larger cells that re-express fetal genes such as ANP and BNP
Sarcomeres added in series, so that each myocyte lengthens
Shrinkage of myocytes with loss of their contractile proteins
approach: Adult cardiomyocytes have largely left the cell cycle and cannot divide in meaningful numbers.
They respond to more work by growing larger (hypertrophy).
A pressure load adds sarcomeres in parallel and turns on a fetal gene program, including ANP, BNP, and beta-myosin heavy chain.
questions.why: Pressure overload stretches myocytes and activates growth signals that increase protein synthesis. Because adult myocytes rarely divide, the heart grows by making each cell larger, not by adding cells. Sarcomeres are added in parallel, which thickens the wall (concentric hypertrophy). The cells also re-express fetal genes such as ANP, BNP, and beta-myosin heavy chain, a slower but more energy-efficient myosin. The thick wall becomes stiff and can outgrow its capillary supply.
whyNot: Adult cardiomyocytes have largely left the cell cycle, so hyperplasia contributes little. This is also why infarcts heal by scar.
Correct.
Sarcomeres added in series lengthen the cells and dilate the chamber. That is eccentric hypertrophy from a volume load, as in aortic regurgitation.
Shrinkage with loss of contractile protein is atrophy, which follows reduced workload or starvation, not increased pressure.

topics: Fetal gene program in the heart

dx: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction in an older woman with isolated systolic hypertension
case: A 78-year-old woman comes to the physician because of progressive shortness of breath on exertion and ankle swelling for 4 months. She has had hypertension for 20 years. Temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 172/68 mmHg. Physical examination shows jugular venous distention, crackles at both lung bases, and pitting edema of both ankles. Serum B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is 640 pg/mL (under 100). A chest radiograph shows upper lobe vascular redistribution and Kerley B lines with a normal-sized cardiac silhouette. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 62% (55 to 70), concentric left ventricular wall thickening, a nondilated left ventricle, impaired relaxation, and an enlarged left atrium. The diagnosis is heart failure with preserved ejection fraction with isolated systolic hypertension.

questions.stem: Compared with a healthy woman of the same age, which of the following best describes her left ventricular end-diastolic volume and end-diastolic pressure?
options: Increased volume and increased pressure
Normal volume and increased pressure
Increased volume and normal pressure
Decreased volume and decreased pressure
approach: Her ejection fraction is normal and her ventricle is not dilated, so this is diastolic dysfunction.
A thick, stiff ventricle needs a higher pressure to fill to the same volume.
The high filling pressure backs up into the left atrium and lungs, causing congestion and a high BNP.
questions.why: In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, the problem is filling, not emptying. Hypertrophy, fibrosis, and slow relaxation make the ventricle stiff, so its end-diastolic pressure-volume curve shifts up and to the left. The chamber fills to a normal or small volume, but only at a high pressure. That pressure is transmitted to the left atrium, which enlarges, and to the pulmonary veins, causing Kerley B lines and crackles.
whyNot: A large volume with high pressure is the pattern of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and a dilated ventricle. Her ventricle is not dilated.
Correct.
A large volume at normal pressure occurs in a compliant ventricle that has adapted to a volume load, such as compensated chronic aortic regurgitation.
Low volume and low pressure occur when the ventricle is underfilled, as in hypovolemia. She has signs of congestion.

topics: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her pulse pressure of 104 mmHg?
options: A large stroke volume ejected by the hypertrophied ventricle
Diastolic backflow through an incompetent aortic valve
Increased arteriolar resistance that raises both pressures
A stiff aorta that poorly buffers each stroke volume
approach: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic pressure: 172 minus 68 is 104 mmHg.
Pulse pressure depends on stroke volume and arterial compliance.

With aging, elastic fibers in the aorta are replaced by collagen, so compliance falls; each normal stroke volume then raises systolic pressure more, and less recoil is left to support diastolic pressure.
questions.why: A compliant aorta stretches during systole and recoils in diastole, which smooths pressure. With age, elastin fragments and collagen increases, so the aorta is stiffer. A normal stroke volume then causes a steeper rise in systolic pressure, and diastolic pressure falls because less energy is stored for recoil. Pulse waves also travel faster and reflect back during systole, adding to the peak. The result is isolated systolic hypertension with a wide pulse pressure, which adds afterload and drives her ventricular hypertrophy.
whyNot: A large stroke volume widens the pulse pressure in high-output states such as fever, anemia, or hyperthyroidism. Nothing here suggests a high-output state, and her low diastolic pressure points to a stiff aorta.
Aortic regurgitation widens pulse pressure, but it causes an early diastolic murmur and a dilated left ventricle. Her ventricle is not dilated.
Higher arteriolar resistance raises mean and diastolic pressures. Her diastolic pressure is low.
Correct.

questions.stem: With the bell of the stethoscope at the apex while she lies in the left lateral decubitus position, a low-pitched sound is heard just before S1. Which of the following best explains this sound?
options: Atrial contraction into a stiff left ventricle
Rapid early filling of a dilated, volume-loaded ventricle
Sudden tensing of chordae under a prolapsing leaflet
Opening of a thickened, fused mitral valve in diastole
approach: A sound just before S1 is in late diastole, which is an S4.
Late diastole is when the atrium contracts.
An S4 means the atrium is pushing blood into a stiff, noncompliant ventricle, which fits her hypertrophy.
questions.why: An S4 is a low-pitched late diastolic sound heard best at the apex with the bell. It is produced when atrial contraction forces blood into a ventricle that cannot stretch easily, and the ventricular wall vibrates. It is typical of hypertensive heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and acute ischemia. An S3, by contrast, occurs in early diastole, just after S2, during rapid filling of a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle.
whyNot: Correct.
Rapid filling of a volume-loaded ventricle causes an S3, which occurs in early diastole just after S2. This sound is just before S1.
Sudden tensing of the chordae causes the midsystolic click of mitral valve prolapse. It falls between S1 and S2.
The opening of a stenotic mitral valve causes an opening snap in early diastole, shortly after S2.

questions.stem: Transesophageal echocardiography gives a clearer view of her enlarged left atrium than the transthoracic study. Which of the following anatomic relationships best explains this?
options: The left atrium forms most of the left border
The left atrium lies just behind the sternum
The left atrium is the most posterior chamber
The left atrium forms the apex of the heart
approach: A transesophageal probe sits in the esophagus, behind the heart.
The left atrium forms most of the base (posterior surface) of the heart.
So the left atrium lies directly in front of the esophagus, with almost nothing in between.
questions.why: The left atrium is the most posterior chamber and lies just anterior to the esophagus. A probe in the esophagus is therefore only millimeters from it, with no lung or rib in the way, so images are sharp. The same relationship explains why a greatly enlarged left atrium can press on the esophagus and cause difficulty swallowing.
whyNot: The left border is formed mainly by the left ventricle, with the left auricle above it. The left atrium is mostly posterior.
The right ventricle is the chamber that lies behind the sternum, forming most of the anterior surface.
Correct.
The apex is formed by the left ventricle and lies near the fifth left intercostal space.

topics: Surfaces and borders of the heart

dx: Orthostatic hypotension from diabetic autonomic neuropathy, with syncope
case: A 61-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus for 35 years comes to the physician because he has fainted twice in the past month when getting out of bed in the morning. He also reports early satiety and erectile dysfunction. Temperature is 36.5 °C (97.7 °F), and respirations are 14/min. Lying supine, his pulse is 76/min and blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg. After 3 minutes of standing, his pulse is 78/min and blood pressure is 106/70 mmHg. Physical examination shows decreased sensation to light touch and vibration in both feet. Hemoglobin A1c is 9.1% (under 5.7). The urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 410 mg/g (under 30). The diagnosis is orthostatic hypotension from diabetic autonomic neuropathy.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the change in his blood pressure on standing?
options: Low blood volume with a normal reflex rise in heart rate
Excess vagal discharge that slows the heart on standing
Pooling of blood in varicose leg veins with leaky valves
Failed sympathetic outflow to the heart and arterioles
approach: Check the definition: a fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing is orthostatic hypotension. His systolic pressure fell 36 mmHg.
Look at the heart rate: it rose only 2/min, so the reflex response is missing.
A missing heart rate rise with long-standing diabetes and other autonomic symptoms points to autonomic failure.
questions.why: Standing pools about 500 mL of blood in the legs and abdomen, lowering venous return and stroke volume. Normally the baroreceptor reflex increases sympathetic activity, which raises heart rate and constricts arterioles and veins within seconds. In diabetic autonomic neuropathy, damage to autonomic fibers blunts this response, so pressure falls with little or no rise in heart rate. His early satiety, which suggests gastroparesis, and his erectile dysfunction are other signs of autonomic damage.
whyNot: Volume depletion, as from vomiting or bleeding, causes orthostatic hypotension with a large rise in heart rate. His heart rate barely changed.
A vasovagal faint involves a sudden fall in heart rate and pressure, often with a trigger and warning symptoms. His heart rate did not fall.
Varicose veins can hold extra blood, but an intact reflex would still raise heart rate and maintain pressure.
Correct.

questions.stem: When he stands, stretch of the receptors at the bifurcation of his common carotid arteries decreases. Which of the following pathways normally carries this change in signaling to the brainstem?
options: Vagus nerve to the nucleus ambiguus
Glossopharyngeal nerve to the nucleus tractus solitarius
Vagus nerve to the nucleus tractus solitarius
Glossopharyngeal nerve to the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
approach: The receptors at the carotid bifurcation are in the carotid sinus.
Their afferent fibers travel in the carotid sinus nerve, a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
All baroreceptor afferents synapse in the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla.
questions.why: The carotid sinus is a dilation at the start of the internal carotid artery. Its stretch receptors send signals through the carotid sinus nerve of CN IX, while aortic arch receptors send signals through CN X. Both end in the nucleus tractus solitarius, which then adjusts vagal output and sympathetic outflow from the medulla. In his neuropathy, the efferent sympathetic limb is the main site of failure.
whyNot: The vagus carries aortic arch baroreceptor signals, not carotid sinus signals. The nucleus ambiguus contains motor neurons, including cardiac vagal neurons, so it is an output, not the afferent target.
Correct.
This is the pathway for the aortic arch baroreceptors. The carotid sinus is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
The nerve is right, but the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus is an efferent parasympathetic nucleus. Sensory baroreceptor fibers end in the nucleus tractus solitarius.

questions.stem: A renal biopsy is performed to evaluate his albuminuria. Both afferent and efferent arterioles show homogeneous, glassy pink thickening of their walls with narrowed lumens. Which of the following best describes this lesion and a biochemical process that contributes to it?
options: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis; smooth muscle growth from severe pressure
Monckeberg sclerosis; calcium phosphate deposited in the media
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis; glycation of basement membrane proteins
Atherosclerosis; oxidized LDL taken up by intimal macrophages
approach: Homogeneous glassy pink thickening of arteriolar walls is hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
In diabetes, chronic high glucose binds proteins without enzymes, forming advanced glycation end products.
Glycated basement membrane proteins trap leaked plasma proteins and promote excess matrix, thickening the wall.
questions.why: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is the arteriolar lesion of diabetes and chronic hypertension. Glucose attaches to long-lived proteins such as basement membrane collagen and forms advanced glycation end products. These cross-link proteins, make the basement membrane leaky, and trap plasma proteins such as albumin in the wall. Involvement of the efferent arteriole is especially typical of diabetes. Atherosclerosis affects large and medium arteries, and Monckeberg sclerosis calcifies the media without narrowing the lumen.
whyNot: Hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis comes from severe, acute hypertension. It shows layered smooth muscle, not homogeneous glassy material.
Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis affects muscular arteries such as those of the legs. It does not narrow the lumen and is not a glassy pink lesion.
Correct.
Atherosclerosis forms intimal plaques in elastic and muscular arteries, not in arterioles.

questions.stem: Two years later, he has a prolonged episode of severe hypotension during sepsis. Afterward, he has weakness of both shoulders and upper arms, with normal strength in his face, hands, and legs. MRI shows bilateral cortical infarcts. Which of the following regions were most likely infarcted?
options: Border zones between the anterior and middle cerebral artery territories
Territories of the lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral arteries
Territories of the anterior cerebral arteries on the medial hemispheres
Border zones between the middle and posterior cerebral artery territories
approach: Global hypotension injures watershed zones first, because they lie at the far ends of two arterial territories.

Bilateral proximal arm weakness with sparing of the face, hands, and legs maps to the part of the motor cortex between the leg area (anterior cerebral artery) and the face and hand area (middle cerebral artery).
That strip is the border zone between the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
questions.why: Watershed areas receive blood from the most distal branches of two arteries, so perfusion pressure there is lowest. When systemic pressure drops, these areas infarct first, often on both sides. The anterior and middle cerebral artery border zone runs along the upper convexity, over the cortex for the shoulder and upper arm. This gives the classic picture of proximal arm weakness on both sides.
whyNot: Correct.
Lenticulostriate infarcts are small, deep lacunar strokes from hypertensive arteriolar disease. They are subcortical and usually one-sided.
Anterior cerebral artery infarcts weaken the leg more than the arm, because the leg area lies on the medial surface.
The middle and posterior cerebral border zone lies in the parieto-occipital region. Infarcts there cause visual and cognitive problems, not shoulder weakness.

dx: Dilated cardiomyopathy in Duchenne muscular dystrophy
case: A 19-year-old man with Duchenne muscular dystrophy comes to the physician because of fatigue, shortness of breath when lying flat, and poor appetite for 2 months. He has used a wheelchair since age 11. Temperature is 36.6 °C (97.9 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 94/62 mmHg. Physical examination shows crackles at both lung bases and an S3 gallop. Serum creatine kinase is 4,800 U/L (40 to 200), and B-type natriuretic peptide is 890 pg/mL (under 100). Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with global hypokinesis. Genetic testing shows a multi-exon deletion in the dystrophin (DMD) gene. The diagnosis is dilated cardiomyopathy in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

questions.stem: His male cousin, the son of his mother's sister, has a deletion of similar size in the same gene, but he walked until age 30 and has only mild weakness at age 35. Which of the following best explains the difference in severity?
options: His deletion shifts the reading frame, so almost no dystrophin is made
His deletion removes the gene's promoter, while his cousin's leaves it intact
His cousin is mosaic, with the deletion present in only some muscle cells
His cousin has a second variant that raises expression of normal dystrophin
approach: Both cousins have X-linked dystrophinopathy from deletions in the same gene.
Severity depends on whether the deletion keeps the reading frame, not on its size.
An out-of-frame deletion causes a premature stop codon and almost no dystrophin (Duchenne); an in-frame deletion makes a shorter, partly working protein (Becker).
questions.why: Dystrophin links the actin cytoskeleton of muscle cells to the dystroglycan complex and the extracellular matrix, protecting the membrane during contraction. In Duchenne dystrophy, a frameshift deletion produces a premature stop codon, and the transcript is degraded, so almost no dystrophin is made. In Becker dystrophy, an in-frame deletion removes some internal amino acids but keeps both ends, so a shortened protein still works partly. Both forms damage cardiac muscle over time, causing fibrosis and dilated cardiomyopathy.
whyNot: Correct.
Most dystrophin deletions are within the coding region, not the promoter. The reading-frame rule explains most differences between Duchenne and Becker.
Mosaicism can lessen disease, but a male who inherits a deletion through his mother carries it in every cell.
No second variant is described. The Becker phenotype is explained by the type of deletion itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of left ventricular findings is most likely on his echocardiogram?
options: Thick walls, a normal ejection fraction, and impaired relaxation
Normal wall thickness, a normal ejection fraction, and impaired filling
Thin walls, a low ejection fraction, and impaired contraction
A thick septum, a high ejection fraction, and outflow obstruction
approach: Dilated cardiomyopathy enlarges all chambers and thins the walls.
Myocyte loss and fibrosis weaken contraction, so the ejection fraction falls (systolic dysfunction).
Compare: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has thick walls and diastolic dysfunction; restrictive cardiomyopathy has stiff, nondilated ventricles with impaired filling.
questions.why: In Duchenne cardiomyopathy, myocytes without dystrophin are damaged by contraction and replaced by fibrous tissue and fat, often starting in the inferolateral wall. The remaining muscle cannot keep up, the ventricle dilates, and the walls become thin relative to the chamber. Contraction is weak and the ejection fraction is low, which is systolic dysfunction. The S3 reflects rapid filling of the large, volume-loaded ventricle.
whyNot: Thick walls with impaired relaxation and a normal ejection fraction describe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or hypertensive heart disease.
A stiff, nondilated ventricle with impaired filling and a preserved ejection fraction fits restrictive cardiomyopathy, as from radiation fibrosis or idiopathic restrictive disease.
Correct.
Asymmetric septal thickening with outflow obstruction is hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, usually from sarcomere gene variants.

questions.stem: Electron micrographs of his ventricular myocardium are compared with those of his skeletal muscle. Which of the following arrangements of T tubules and sarcoplasmic reticulum is expected in the cardiac muscle?
options: T tubules at the A-I junction, each flanked by two cisternae
T tubules at the Z line, each paired with one cisterna
No T tubules, with caveolae beside the sarcoplasmic reticulum
T tubules at the H band, each flanked by two cisternae
approach: Skeletal muscle has triads: one T tubule between two terminal cisternae at each A-I junction.
Cardiac muscle has wider T tubules located at the Z lines.
Each cardiac T tubule usually meets one small cisterna of sarcoplasmic reticulum, forming a diad.
questions.why: In cardiac muscle, T tubules enter at the Z lines and pair with a single expansion of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, forming diads. The cardiac sarcoplasmic reticulum is less developed than in skeletal muscle, so calcium entering through L-type channels is needed to trigger further calcium release. Other differences include branched cells, one or two central nuclei, and intercalated discs with fascia adherens, desmosomes, and gap junctions.
whyNot: Triads at the A-I junction are the arrangement in skeletal muscle, which is the comparison sample.
Correct.
Smooth muscle lacks T tubules and uses caveolae near a sparse sarcoplasmic reticulum.
No T tubules sit at the H band. The H band is the central zone of the A band where only thick filaments are present.

questions.stem: During an arm-crank exercise test, his O2 uptake rises from 250 mL/min at rest to 600 mL/min at peak exercise, and his cardiac output rises from 4.0 L/min to 5.0 L/min. Which of the following is closest to his arteriovenous O2 difference at peak exercise?
options: About 5.0 mL O2/dL
About 6.3 mL O2/dL
About 9.0 mL O2/dL
About 12 mL O2/dL
approach: Rearrange the Fick principle: arteriovenous O2 difference equals O2 uptake divided by cardiac output.
At peak, 600 mL/min divided by 50 dL/min is 12 mL O2/dL.
Compare with rest (250 divided by 40 is about 6.3 mL O2/dL): the difference nearly doubled because his cardiac output could rise only 25%.
questions.why: O2 uptake is the product of cardiac output and arteriovenous O2 difference. In healthy people, both rise during exercise, with cardiac output rising several-fold. His weak, dilated ventricle cannot raise stroke volume much, so his cardiac output barely increases. To meet the higher demand, his muscles must extract more O2 from each deciliter of blood, so the arteriovenous difference widens and mixed venous O2 falls.
whyNot: This mixes resting and peak values: resting O2 uptake (250 mL/min) divided by peak cardiac output (50 dL/min).
This is his resting arteriovenous difference (250 divided by 40). The question asks about peak exercise.
This value would need a peak cardiac output of about 6.7 L/min, which he did not reach.
Correct.

dx: Left atrial myxoma with an embolic stroke
case: A 52-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of right facial and arm weakness and difficulty speaking. For 3 months she has had fatigue, low-grade fevers, a 5-kg weight loss, and shortness of breath and lightheadedness when she sits up. Temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg. Physical examination shows a right facial droop, right arm weakness, and expressive aphasia. Hemoglobin is 10.9 g/dL (12 to 16), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 68 mm/h (0 to 30). MRI shows an acute left middle cerebral artery infarct. Echocardiography shows a 5-cm mobile left atrial mass attached by a stalk to the interatrial septum that prolapses through the mitral valve in diastole. The diagnosis is left atrial myxoma with an embolic stroke.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her fever, weight loss, anemia, and increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate?
options: Bacterial infection of the tumor surface that seeds the blood
Metastatic spread of tumor cells into the bone marrow
Interleukin 6 secreted by the tumor cells
Immune complexes against tumor antigens deposited in vessels
approach: Myxoma is a benign tumor, so constitutional symptoms are not from metastasis.
Many myxomas secrete interleukin 6.
Interleukin 6 drives the acute phase response: fever, weight loss, high fibrinogen (raising the sedimentation rate), and hepcidin-mediated anemia of inflammation.
questions.why: Atrial myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults. It is usually a pedunculated, gelatinous mass on the left atrial side of the septum. Besides ball-valve obstruction and emboli, it often causes systemic symptoms because the tumor cells secrete interleukin 6. Interleukin 6 causes fever, increases hepatic acute phase proteins such as fibrinogen and hepcidin, and leads to anemia of inflammation. These symptoms usually resolve after the tumor is removed.
whyNot: Infection of a myxoma is rare. A bacterial cause would be expected to produce positive blood cultures and a picture of endocarditis.
Myxomas are benign and do not metastasize. Fragments can embolize, but this is not metastatic spread to marrow.
Correct.
Immune complex deposition explains some findings in infective endocarditis and lupus, such as glomerulonephritis. It is not the main mechanism of myxoma symptoms.

topics: Interleukin 6 and the acute phase response

questions.stem: The stalk is attached to the left atrial side of the interatrial septum at the edge of a thin region that was an open passage before birth. Which of the following structures marks this same region on the right atrial side?
options: Crista terminalis
Opening of the coronary sinus
Pectinate muscles of the auricle
Fossa ovalis
approach: The fetal passage between the atria is the foramen ovale.
After birth, the septum primum flap seals it, leaving a thin area in the septum.
On the right atrial side, this thin area is the oval depression called the fossa ovalis.
questions.why: Before birth, the foramen ovale lets oxygen-rich blood pass from the right atrium to the left atrium. After birth, left atrial pressure rises and pushes the septum primum against the septum secundum, closing the passage. The fossa ovalis is the depression that remains on the right atrial side, and its raised margin is the limbus. Most myxomas arise from the septum near this region, usually on the left side.
whyNot: The crista terminalis is a muscular ridge in the right atrium that separates its smooth posterior part from the pectinate part. It is not on the septum.
The coronary sinus opens into the right atrium between the inferior vena cava opening and the tricuspid valve. It is not a fetal passage.
Pectinate muscles are ridges in the right auricle and the anterior right atrial wall, not on the septum.
Correct.

topics: Internal features of the right atrium

questions.stem: If the same tumor had arisen in the right atrium of a patient with an intact atrial septum, fragments breaking off from it would most likely lodge in which of the following vessels?
options: Pulmonary arteries
Middle cerebral arteries
Renal arteries
Splenic arteries
approach: An embolus travels downstream until it reaches a vessel too small to pass.
From the right atrium, blood goes through the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.
With no shunt, right-sided emboli lodge in the pulmonary arteries.
questions.why: The route of an embolus depends on where it starts. Emboli from the left heart, such as from this left atrial myxoma or a mural thrombus, enter the systemic arteries and lodge in the brain, legs, gut, kidneys, or spleen. Emboli from the right heart or systemic veins go to the lungs. A right-sided embolus can reach the systemic circulation only through a right-to-left shunt, such as a patent foramen ovale, which is called a paradoxical embolus.
whyNot: Correct.
Her left atrial tumor reached the middle cerebral artery. A right atrial tumor would reach the brain only through a right-to-left shunt, which this patient does not have.
The renal arteries receive emboli from the left heart or aorta, not from the right atrium.
The spleen is a common site for systemic emboli from the left heart, not for right-sided emboli.

questions.stem: Before her stroke, auscultation at the apex revealed a low-pitched early diastolic sound followed by a rumbling murmur that changed with her body position. This murmur most closely resembles that of which of the following lesions, and why?
options: Mitral regurgitation, because the mass keeps the leaflets from closing in systole
Mitral stenosis, because the mass obstructs inflow during diastolic filling
Aortic regurgitation, because the mass distorts the aortic root in diastole
Aortic stenosis, because the mass narrows the outflow tract in systole
approach: Time the murmur: a rumble after an early diastolic sound at the apex is a mid-diastolic murmur.
A mid-diastolic apical rumble comes from turbulent flow across a narrowed mitral orifice.
Here the mass plugs the mitral orifice when it prolapses in diastole, and the early sound is the tumor plop as it moves into the valve.
questions.why: A mobile left atrial myxoma swings into the mitral orifice during diastole and blocks inflow, much like mitral stenosis. This produces a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, often preceded by a tumor plop that can be mistaken for an opening snap. Because the mass moves with gravity, the murmur and symptoms change with position. Sitting up lets the tumor fall into the valve, which explains her positional dyspnea and lightheadedness.
whyNot: Mitral regurgitation causes a holosystolic murmur at the apex. This murmur is diastolic.
Correct.
Aortic regurgitation causes an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border, not an apical rumble. A left atrial mass does not involve the aortic root.
Aortic stenosis causes a crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border. This murmur is diastolic.

dx: Anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) in a 2-month-old infant
case: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of poor feeding and weight gain for 3 weeks. His mother says he sweats, cries, and becomes pale during feeds. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 168/min, respirations are 62/min, and blood pressure is 78/44 mmHg. Physical examination shows a liver edge palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin and a holosystolic murmur at the apex. An ECG shows deep, wide Q waves in leads I and aVL. Echocardiography shows a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 28% (55 to 70) and retrograde flow from the left coronary artery into the pulmonary trunk. The diagnosis is anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA).

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his symptoms began weeks after birth rather than at delivery?
options: The ductus arteriosus closed, removing his main source of coronary flow
Pulmonary artery pressure fell, so flow into the left coronary dropped
The foramen ovale closed, lowering the O2 saturation of left atrial blood
Fetal hemoglobin was replaced, reducing O2 release to the myocardium
approach: Before birth, pulmonary artery pressure is about equal to aortic pressure, so the anomalous artery is well perfused.
After birth, pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure fall over several weeks.
The left coronary is then perfused at low pressure with desaturated blood, and once collaterals form, blood flows backward from the left coronary into the pulmonary trunk (coronary steal).
questions.why: In the fetus, the ductus arteriosus links the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, and pulmonary and systemic pressures are nearly equal. After birth, lung expansion and higher O2 lower pulmonary vascular resistance, and pulmonary artery pressure falls over the first weeks. The anomalous left coronary then fills poorly with desaturated blood. Collaterals from the right coronary develop, but blood follows the low-pressure path back into the pulmonary trunk, stealing flow from the myocardium. Feeding raises O2 demand and causes ischemic pain, which shows as crying, sweating, and pallor.
whyNot: The ductus carries blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta in the fetus. Its closure does not remove a coronary blood supply.
Correct.
Closure of the foramen ovale stops right-to-left atrial flow, which raises, not lowers, the O2 saturation of left-sided blood.
Adult hemoglobin has a lower O2 affinity than fetal hemoglobin, so it releases O2 more easily to tissues.

questions.stem: Before birth, the blood entering his anomalous left coronary artery was less oxygenated than the blood entering his normally placed right coronary artery. Which of the following best explains this difference?
options: Placental blood crossed the foramen ovale; SVC blood went to the right ventricle
The ductus venosus carried placental blood directly into the pulmonary trunk
The ductus arteriosus carried oxygen-rich aortic blood back into the pulmonary trunk
The umbilical arteries returned oxygen-rich placental blood into the right atrium
approach: Oxygen-rich blood from the placenta travels in the umbilical vein, through the ductus venosus, into the inferior vena cava.
In the right atrium, this stream is directed through the foramen ovale to the left atrium, left ventricle, and ascending aorta, which feeds the coronaries and brain.
Desaturated blood from the superior vena cava goes through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk, which fed his anomalous artery.
questions.why: Fetal circulation keeps two streams partly separate. The better-oxygenated inferior vena cava stream, carrying placental blood, is directed by the edge of the septum secundum through the foramen ovale into the left heart. It is ejected into the ascending aorta, so the normal coronary arteries and the brain get the best-oxygenated blood. The superior vena cava stream, which is poorly oxygenated, goes to the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk, and most of it crosses the ductus arteriosus to the descending aorta. An artery arising from the pulmonary trunk receives this less oxygenated blood.
whyNot: Correct.
The ductus venosus carries umbilical venous blood past the liver into the inferior vena cava, not into the pulmonary trunk.
Fetal ductal flow runs from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, because pulmonary resistance is high. It does not send aortic blood into the pulmonary trunk.
The umbilical arteries carry desaturated blood from the fetus to the placenta. They do not return blood to the heart.

topics: Streaming in the fetal right atrium

questions.stem: At 2 months of age, his pulmonary artery pressure is 24/10 mmHg while his aortic pressure is 78/44 mmHg, although both circuits carry nearly the same blood flow. Which of the following best explains the lower pressure in his pulmonary circuit?
options: Thicker smooth muscle in pulmonary arterioles that limits flow
A smaller stroke volume ejected by the right ventricle
Greater compliance of systemic arteries than pulmonary arteries
Low resistance from many short, wide, thin-walled vessels
approach: Pressure drop equals flow times resistance.
Flow through the lungs equals flow through the body, so a lower pressure means a lower resistance.
Pulmonary vessels are short, wide, and thin-walled with little smooth muscle, and many capillaries can be recruited or distended, so resistance is low.
questions.why: The right and left ventricles pump nearly the same output in series, so the pressure difference between the circuits comes from resistance. Pulmonary vascular resistance is a small fraction of systemic resistance because the pulmonary arteries are short and wide, their arterioles have little smooth muscle, and the capillary bed is large. When flow rises, closed capillaries open (recruitment) and open ones widen (distension), so resistance falls and pressure rises only a little. After birth, the fall in this resistance is what lowered the pressure feeding his anomalous artery.
whyNot: Pulmonary arterioles have less smooth muscle than systemic arterioles. Thick muscle would raise resistance and pressure.
Right and left ventricular stroke volumes are equal over time, because the circuits are in series.
Pulmonary arteries are more compliant than systemic arteries. Compliance affects pulse pressure more than mean pressure.
Correct.

questions.stem: During feeding, his myocardial O2 demand rises. In the territory of his normal right coronary artery, flow increases through local metabolic control. Which of the following best describes the main metabolic vasodilator and why flow, rather than O2 extraction, must increase?
options: Adenosine from ATP breakdown; extraction can still triple with demand
Lactate from glycolysis; extraction can still triple with demand
Adenosine from ATP breakdown; extraction is near maximal at rest
Nitric oxide from L-arginine; extraction is near maximal at rest
approach: When O2 demand outpaces supply, ATP is broken down to ADP and AMP, and 5'-nucleotidase converts AMP to adenosine.
Adenosine diffuses to coronary arterioles and relaxes their smooth muscle.
The heart already extracts about 70 to 80% of arterial O2 at rest, so extra demand can be met only by more flow.
questions.why: Coronary flow is matched to myocardial metabolism. As ATP use rises, AMP accumulates and is dephosphorylated to adenosine, which acts on A2A receptors on arteriolar smooth muscle to cause dilation. Low O2, high CO2, H+, and K+ add to the effect. Because the myocardium already removes most of the O2 from coronary blood at rest, coronary sinus blood is very desaturated, and there is little room to extract more. In ALCAPA, the anomalous territory cannot increase flow, so ischemia appears with feeding.
whyNot: Adenosine is right, but the heart cannot triple its extraction. It already removes most of the O2 at rest, unlike skeletal muscle.
Lactate rises during ischemia but is not the main coronary vasodilator, and the extraction statement is wrong.
Correct.
Nitric oxide is an endothelial vasodilator that responds to shear stress and acetylcholine. It is not the main metabolic signal linking demand to flow.
